name: AI and Authorship
title: AI and Authorship
answer: AI and authorship concerns who or what counts as an author when generative models contribute to text, code, images, or research outputs. It covers attribution, credit, plagiarism, and the integrity of scholarly and creative records. The page examines policies from journals, funders, and institutions on disclosing AI assistance and distinguishing human from machine contribution. It also addresses the limits of current definitions of authorship when a system can draft, revise, or generate ideas.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: AI and authorship concerns who or what counts as an author when generative models contribute to text, code, images, or research outputs. It covers attribution, credit, plagiarism, and the integrity of scholarly and creative records. The page examines policies from journals, funders, and institutions on disclosing AI assistance and distinguishing human from machine contribution. It also addresses the limits of current definitions of authorship when a system can draft, revise, or generate ideas.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work of determining authorship runs on document corpora, version histories, metadata standards, and provenance logs rather than on a single model. Research integrity systems use plagiarism detectors, text similarity tools, and sometimes stylometric or watermarking methods to flag machine-generated passages. These tools operate on institutional repositories, preprint servers, and publisher submission platforms. The site's library of research papers and extracted claims provides a base for tracing how authorship norms are documented, but the page itself does not run models.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners typically compare a submitted work against known human and machine writing patterns, check disclosure statements, and review contribution records. Some workflows use fine-tuned classifiers or perplexity scores to estimate the likelihood that a passage was generated by a large language model. Human editors and integrity officers then adjudicate borderline cases, because automated flags are not proof of authorship. The method is therefore a mix of computational screening and human judgment.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on misattribution, ghost authorship, and the erosion of accountability when a machine cannot take responsibility for errors or harm. Many journals now require authors to declare any use of AI in drafting or analysis, and some prohibit listing an AI system as an author. Risks include false accusations based on unreliable detectors, loss of trust in peer review, and unclear ownership of AI-assisted outputs. Provenance records, such as versioned drafts and tool logs, are becoming part of responsible practice, though no universal standard exists.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward finer-grained contribution taxonomies, such as distinguishing ideation, drafting, editing, and verification, rather than a binary human or machine label. Publishers and funders are likely to adopt machine-readable disclosure formats and persistent provenance trails. As models become better at mimicking individual style, detection will become less reliable, pushing the emphasis toward verified process records and institutional norms. The long-term question is whether authorship itself will shift from a property of individuals to a property of documented workflows.
